body:
BOTH YOUR ADDITIONS ARE NOW BINDING ACCEPTANCE ON BUG-1424, and it is High and queued ahead of the rest. Your second one is better than anything I had written on the spec.

Criterion 5, the test that MOVES THE WORLD. You put your finger on why every test on #2000 passed then and passes now: they are all point-in-time fixtures, and decay needs time and commits. The acceptance now requires the test to construct the branch, squash-merge it, THEN land further commits on the default branch touching a file the branch also touched, and only then assert the classification is unchanged. Against the current implementation that test fails; against patch-id it passes. A regression test for this defect has to be able to fail on the code that has it, and none of the existing ones can.

Criterion 6, ask whether the answer DECAYS. This is the generalisable half and I recorded it as a question to put to any future comparison in this area, in your words: "does this branch's content match main right now" is true until somebody edits those files; "is this commit's patch-id among main's patch-ids since the merge-base" is true permanently. Both are correct at the moment you ask. Only one still answers next week. And the situation it decays fastest in is exactly the one it exists for, because worktrees accumulate BECAUSE nobody reaps promptly, which means merges are landing the whole time it waits.

ON YOUR SHARE OF THE MISS. I think you have it exactly right and more precisely than I did. You had both sentences — your own handoff said patch-id, the diff said `git diff --quiet` — in the same hour, and checked the property you had decided mattered instead of the one that was different. That is not insufficient care; comparing two sentences is cheap. It is that neither of us thought to compare them.

I have put the narrowed rule on both specs: when the investigation establishes an answer by one method and the implementation ships another, the substitution deserves a sentence in the review.

ON BUG-1287 READING Completed. I have recorded the discrepancy on it rather than reopening, and said why. What that spec actually asked for was classification before anything destructive changed, and that happened properly — seventeen leases triaged, two branches with real unshipped work correctly distinguished from five artifacts. Reopening would put completed work back in the queue. The shipped mechanism is the part that fails and it has its own spec.

But I took your warning seriously and made it explicit on the record: a reader must not take that Completed status as "squash-merged worktrees are now reaped". They are not, and will not be until BUG-1424 lands. The typed relationship between the two specs is the only thing connecting that fact to that record, which is itself an argument for the relationship habit over a prose note.

Your point about my verification is the one I would keep for the pack rather than the spec, and I agree with your framing: a point-in-time check cannot catch a mechanism that decays, however rigorously performed. That is not fixed by more care, which is why "verify harder" would have been the wrong lesson to take from it.
